cls: Herbal medicinal product (standardised Ginkgo biloba leaf extract)
pharm: Standardised extract of Ginkgo biloba leaves (e.g., EGb 761) used as a herbal medicine for cognitive symptoms and circulatory complaints; contains flavonoid glycosides and terpene lactones (ginkgolides, bilobalide).
quick: Standardised extract (e.g., EGb 761) commonly 120-240 mg per day in divided doses
May be taken with or without food
Not recommended - insufficient data and possible bleeding/uterine effects
No specific adjustment at usual doses
No specific adjustment; caution with hepatotoxic co-medication
Bleeding/bruising (especially with antithrombotics), seizure control, response
summary: Ginkgo biloba extract is a standardised herbal preparation of Ginkgo leaf (the best-studied being EGb 761), standardised to about 24% flavonoid glycosides and 6% terpene lactones (ginkgolides and bilobalide). It is used as a herbal medicine for symptoms of mild cognitive impairment/age-related memory complaints and dementia, and for circulatory complaints such as intermittent claudication, vertigo, and tinnitus, though evidence is mixed. Typical adult dosing is 120-240 mg of standardised extract daily in divided doses. It is generally well tolerated, but the most clinically important concern is an increased risk of BLEEDING, particularly when combined with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs; ginkgo seeds and crude leaf (not the standardised extract) can contain toxic/allergenic constituents. It is not an FDA-approved drug and is regulated as a herbal/dietary product.
indications: Symptoms of mild age-related cognitive impairment and memory complaints (herbal use)
Adjunct in mild-to-moderate dementia (Alzheimer/vascular) symptom support (evidence mixed)
Peripheral arterial disease / intermittent claudication (herbal use)
Vertigo and tinnitus of vascular origin (herbal use)

Use a reputable standardised extract (flavonoid glycosides and terpene lactones quantified); avoid crude leaf preparations and never consume ginkgo seeds
Allow several weeks of regular use before judging benefit

moa: The pharmacological activity of standardised Ginkgo biloba extract is attributed mainly to flavonoid glycosides (antioxidant, free-radical scavenging) and terpene lactones - ginkgolides (platelet-activating factor antagonists) and bilobalide. Proposed mechanisms include improved microcirculation and blood flow, reduced blood viscosity, antagonism of platelet-activating factor (contributing to antiplatelet effects), neuroprotective and antioxidant actions, and modulation of neurotransmitter systems. These effects underlie its traditional use for cognitive and circulatory complaints, although the clinical evidence is inconsistent.

relative: Concurrent anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy (bleeding risk)
Upcoming surgery or dental procedures (stop beforehand)
Seizure disorders (case reports of seizures, especially with contaminated/crude products)
monitor: Bleeding and bruising, particularly with antithrombotic drugs

preg: Use during pregnancy is not recommended owing to insufficient safety data and theoretical concerns about platelet/bleeding effects (including at delivery). Avoid unless advised by a healthcare professional.
lact: There are insufficient data on Ginkgo biloba during breastfeeding; use is not recommended. Weigh any perceived benefit against the lack of safety information.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required at usual herbal doses; there are no significant renal handling concerns reported for the standardised extract.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established at usual doses. Use caution if combined with potentially hepatotoxic medicines and monitor for any signs of liver injury.

major: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs) - increased bleeding risk; avoid or monitor closely
moderate: Antiseizure drugs - ginkgo (especially contaminated/crude products) may lower seizure threshold and reduce anticonvulsant efficacy
Drugs metabolised by CYP2C9/CYP3A4 - ginkgo may alter levels of some drugs (e.g., some reports with omeprazole, efavirenz, certain statins); review
Other herbs/supplements that increase bleeding (fish oil, garlic, vitamin E) - additive effect
minor: May theoretically interact with antidiabetic agents (variable effects on insulin/glucose) - monitor glucose
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no specific food restrictions for the standardised extract.
interactions.diagnostics: No routine monitoring required; consider bleeding-risk awareness (INR/clinical bleeding) if combined with antithrombotics.

serious: Bleeding events (including reports of intracranial and ocular bleeding), especially with antithrombotic drugs

monitoring: Signs of bleeding or easy bruising, especially with anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs
Seizure control in patients with epilepsy
Clinical response over several weeks for cognitive/circulatory symptoms
counsel: This is a herbal medicine, not a licensed prescription drug - tell your doctor and pharmacist you are taking it
It can increase the risk of bleeding - mention it if you take blood thinners or aspirin, and stop it 1-2 weeks before any surgery
Use a standardised extract from a reputable source; never eat ginkgo seeds and avoid crude leaf products
If you have epilepsy, check with your doctor first, as ginkgo has been linked to seizures
Give it several weeks to see any effect, and report unusual bleeding, severe headache, or allergic reactions
pk: Symptomatic effects, if any, develop gradually over weeks of regular use
Active constituents reach peak plasma levels within 1-3 hours of dosing
Terpene lactones have half-lives of roughly 3-10 hours; flavonoids vary
Divided daily dosing maintains levels; clinical benefit requires sustained use
Store in a cool, dry place away from light and moisture; keep in the original container
pearls: Not FDA-approved as a drug - Ginkgo biloba is a herbal medicinal product (best evidence with the standardised extract EGb 761); guidance follows EMA/HMPC herbal monographs and herbal references, not an FDA drug label
The key clinical safety issue is BLEEDING risk - avoid or monitor closely with anticoagulants/antiplatelets and stop before surgery
Use only standardised extracts (about 24% flavonoid glycosides, 6% terpene lactones); ginkgo SEEDS are toxic and crude products may contain ginkgolic acids/contaminants linked to seizures and allergy
Evidence for cognitive and circulatory benefit is mixed and not definitive
Caution in epilepsy (reported seizures) and review potential CYP-mediated drug interactions
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember, or skip it and continue your usual schedule - do not double up. As a herbal supplement, an occasional missed dose is not harmful.
overdose: Overdose data are limited; large amounts may cause gastrointestinal upset, restlessness, weakness, and theoretically increased bleeding. Ingestion of ginkgo SEEDS (not the leaf extract) can cause serious toxicity including seizures, especially in children. There is no specific antidote; provide supportive care, manage seizures with standard measures, and seek emergency care for significant ingestions, particularly of seeds or in children.
